Risk Management ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 15:02 Households once ran on a checkbook, a stamp, and a Saturday trip to the bank. Could your company run that way again if it had to? November 19, 2026 Image On Dec. 18, Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters, and millions of us will happily pay to watch Earth's mightiest heroes face a villain bent on bringing the world to its knees. It's a great escape, partly because we know the heroes always show up in time. Real life offers no such guarantee, and last week showed how close we already live to our own doomsday script. Consider how recently the world ran on paper. Not long ago, people received a printed paycheck every week. Many of us remember our parents planning lunch hours around getting to the bank, or racing there Saturday morning before the branch closed at noon. Bills were paid by paper check, mailed to the mortgage company, the electric company and the oil company. Insuring a car or a house meant calling an agent. Buying anything "from a computer" was pure Isaac Asimov. Today, the entirety of human knowledge fits in a device the size of a deck of cards that nearly everyone carries in their pocket. That has been liberating. But it has also left us almost completely dependent on invisible systems we assume will always be on and safe from disruption, whether the threat is a malfunction, a cyberattack or simple human error. The past week showed how quickly those systems can grind to a halt. On Nov. 12, a Microsoft outage took down Outlook, Teams and Copilot – the backbone of millions of businesses – across dozens of countries for more than half a day. The next afternoon, a communications failure forced the FAA to ground every departing U.S. flight for more than four hours, the longest nationwide shutdown since 9/11. Then on Nov. 16, a software bug in JPMorgan Chase's own hardware disrupted online banking, branch transactions and Zelle payments, spilling over to customers at other banks doing business with Chase. Chase said there was no evidence the outage was cyber-related, and that is exactly the point. If an internal glitch can rattle America's biggest commercial bank, imagine what a deliberate, coordinated attack on power grids, water systems and communications networks could do. Governments urge households to keep emergency supplies, including cash, on hand. Is your company following the same advice? Do business continuity plans cover this? For many companies, the honest answer is "not really." Most plans are built for hurricanes, fires, the loss of a building and other localized events. Backups reside in another state, employees work from home, and operations shift to a recovery site. All of this assumes the Internet, the power grid, and the rest of the economy are still working somewhere . Financial regulators have pushed for more. In 2019, the FFIEC reframed its guidance from business continuity planning to business continuity management, with a focus on operational resilience and the ripple effects of outages across the financial system. The industry also created Sheltered Harbor , a standard for backing up critical customer account data nightly to an offline, air-gapped vault so customers can still reach their funds after a worst-case cyber event. Sheltered Harbor is now winding down, with its specification moving to its parent, FS-ISAC, but the principle stands. Still, even these measures assume someone, somewhere, can restore the data and run the systems. A nationwide, prolonged outage is a scenario few plans address head-on. Can companies function when the rest of the world can't? Not entirely. If customers can't reach essential services, payment rails are down and vendors go dark, no amount of preparation will preserve business as usual. But "not entirely" is materially different from "not at all." The goal is keeping your promises: knowing who your customers are, what they own and what you owe them, and honoring the most critical obligations through manual processes until systems return. That is what makes recovery possible, and it preserves trust when it matters most. Building on the plan you already have Organizations don't need to start over. They need to extend the plans they already have: Add a "dark scenario." Model a weeklong nationwide Internet and communications outage combined with an attack that corrupts your own backups. Ask what breaks first. Define minimum viable operations. For an insurer, that may mean confirming coverage, taking claims, and issuing emergency payments for catastrophic losses. For a bank, it may be cash access, balance verification, and critical payments. Everything else can wait. Keep offline, immutable copies of critical data. Maintain air-gapped backups, plus periodic printed records of policies, account balances, and key contacts. Bring back the manual playbook. Stock paper claim forms and check stock, set pre-approved emergency payment limits and clear signatory authority, and keep the procedures in print. Give a defined role to people with institutional memory of how the work got done before your digital transformation. Plan communications without the Internet. Think satellite phones, two-way radios, pre-arranged meeting points, and agreements with local broadcasters to reach customers. Pressure-test your vendors. Your plan is only as strong as your cloud providers, core processors and payment networks. Know what each would do in this scenario. Take care of your people. Employees will face the same disruption at home. Plan for staff who can't get to work, need cash, or must care for their families. Practice it. Run tabletop exercises in which nothing digital works. Gaps found in a conference room cost far less than gaps found in a crisis. Will you really be there? Nearly every bank and insurance ad promises some version of "we're there when you need us." Those promises were written with storms, fires, and floods in mind. But a slogan has no fine print. When the screens go dark, customers will expect the companies that made those promises to show up. Insurers, whose very reason for being is to anticipate the worst, are well placed to lead, both by hardening their own operations and by helping clients understand how their coverage would respond to a systemic event. Would a cyber or business interruption policy respond to a days-long cloud outage that wasn't caused by an attack? To a bank glitch that delays payroll? After last week, many risk managers are likely asking those questions for the first time. Insurers and brokers with clear answers ready will earn trust before the next outage arrives. In the end, a policy or a bank account is a promise, and trust is what customers are really buying. A company that goes silent in a crisis may never regain it. One that shows up, even with a pen, a paper form, and a phone tree, will be remembered for it. Is it really possible to be fully prepared? No organization can solve everything a large-scale shutdown would throw at it. But there is a big difference between a plan that misses a few angles and one undone by what the 9/11 Commission called a "failure of imagination." The organizations that have thought it through, protected their data, and kept manual workflows open will be the ones that help their customers first and recover fastest. In the movies, doomsday is averted by heroes in capes. In real life, it will be survived thanks to the continuity planner with a binder of printed procedures, the claims veteran who remembers how to cut a paper check, and the IT lead who already knows which vendor to call. They are the real superheroes. Now is the time to give them what they need. Households once ran on a checkbook, a stamp, and a Saturday trip to the bank. Could your company run that way again if it had to? Diane Brassard James Ballot

why_it_matters.en: Insurers and financial institutions must reassess their business continuity plans to address potential nationwide outages and ensure they can meet customer obligations during crises. This includes maintaining critical data offline and preparing for manual operations in the event of system failures.
why_it_matters.zh: 这类监管更新可能改变报告口径、资本约束或合规流程。精算人应关注模型假设、披露要求和管理层行动是否需要同步调整。
why_it_matters.fr: Cette évolution peut modifier les exigences de reporting, de capital ou de gouvernance. Les actuaires doivent vérifier les impacts sur les hypothèses, les contrôles et les livrables réglementaires.

items.actuarial_angle: 可能改变核保、定价、理赔、反欺诈、客户运营和模型治理方式。
actions: 判断技术处于概念验证、试点、规模化还是监管约束阶段。
列出一个可落地场景：数据输入、模型输出、业务决策、风险控制。
检查模型风险：公平性、可解释性、漂移监控、人工复核和数据授权。

items.title: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline
items.original_title: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline
items.rss_title: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline
items.rss_description: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline Talent Gap ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 11:05 As AI automates entry-level insurance tasks, insurance industry leaders must design experiences to develop professional judgment in emerging talent. November 19, 2026 Image Back in the '90s, I was a beast at reconciling spreadsheets. The 10 fingers I'm using to type these lines used to set my "10-key" numeric keypad ablaze. But if you're among the younger readers to come across this article, you'll have no idea what I'm talking about. And as a society, I think that's for the best. A core promise of technological advancement is to eliminate drudgery, like using a 10-key to enter vast amounts of numeric data. In property and casualty insurance, we have spent decades trying to remove mundane work from the lives of underwriters, claims professionals, and technologists. We made great strides with Robotic Process Automation (RPA), leaps with broader Intelligent Automation (IA), and now a phenomenal bound with Artificial Intelligence (AI), which promises to revolutionize the way we work. But amid the terrific change lurks an industry-scale problem. While our job definitions and related skills are morphing at an absurdly fast rate, how do we ensure that emerging talent has the opportunity to develop the depth of understanding and judgment their predecessors possess, even while AI is tending to disassociate humans from some of the traditional activities of their craft? That replacement system needs a name and, more importantly, an owner. Architecting Experience is the framework of deliberately designed exposures, decisions, and feedback loops through which people develop professional judgment and decision context. Cracks in the career ladder Stanford's Digital Economy Lab analyzed payroll data on millions of U.S. jobs through June 2026 and found no economy-wide displacement from AI. What they did find was new employment among 22- to 25-year-olds lagging in industries heavily affected by AI, by about 19% compared to less-affected industries.[1] The employment ladder isn't broken, but some rungs at the bottom are disappearing, which makes it a whole lot harder to climb. Even where junior positions aren't disappearing, the formative skills they help develop are the easiest to automate. In insurance, applied experience and apprenticeship have built the tacit knowledge and judgment needed for success for generations. After ingesting enough submissions, you develop a second sense for when a detail looks off, or when risks that look identical stem from entirely different causes. But when this repetitive and seemingly menial work is delegated to AI, younger staff are deprived of the very task-level experiences they need to develop the business EQ, empathy, and scar tissue that will someday make them senior. What our young talent are left with are the tasks too difficult for AI, and sometimes beyond the judgment they possess. In their 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, PwC looked at over a billion job advertisements. They found that heavily AI-exposed entry-level roles were seven times more likely to demand senior capabilities—like judgment, leadership, and interpersonal skills—than the jobs least exposed to AI. PwC described the trend as the "seniorization" of junior work.[2] A short-term view of AI-driven task optimization will only make the problem worse. For senior employees, more demanding tasks feel more meaningful and engaging than rote work. But the type of work that is most interesting to a seasoned professional isn't necessarily the type of work best suited to creating one. And meaningful work sounds wonderful until every task is a demanding one, and the much-needed Easy Tuesday becomes as much of a relic as my most trusty 10-digit keypad. Clear the slop from the stream BCG recently surveyed 11,749 workers across 14 markets about their use of AI at work. Two-thirds of regular AI users reported increased job satisfaction. At the same time, 41% reported increased mental strain. Half said they were spending more time managing and directing AI than doing the underlying work itself.[3] "Brain fry" refers to the mental fatigue associated with information overload from increased AI oversight.[4] With AI, any junior underwriter can generate a 40-page report with the aplomb of a managing director. But then, the report has to be checked. Preferably by someone with enough know-how to identify and correct mistakes. Without guardrails, we quickly end up in a system where our young talent can access AI-powered tools that allow them to produce work that looks good, but is actually riddled with problems. These problems are then sent upstream to more senior resources who have to spend their time fixing this "workslop"[5]. Junior professionals learn nothing in the process, and increase the workload of their most knowledgeable, and often most expensive, colleagues. When we claim AI is changing the way we work, we're giving the tool too much credit, while absolving ourselves of responsibility. The truth is, AI isn't changing the way we work. Our decision-makers are. And if, as a result of these changes and the adoption of AI, the leaders break the career ladder, they are responsible for engineering a new one. AI-resilient architecture I'm not in favor of clinging to rote work out of nostalgia. AI very much has a place in our workflows, and I remain bullish on the beneficial role of AI over the long term. But today, as we are all still sorting out the impacts and influences of AI on real people, we must think things through holistically and humanistically from the very beginning. In the face of AI removing traditional and lower-level tasks, the implications of this must be assessed, and solutions for the resultant gaps must be created. When architecting experience for new talent, what matters is to look at tasks through the dual lens of raw efficiency and professional development. Do the tasks teach the rules of the game, and more importantly, when the rules stop applying? Do they offer a chance to shadow a more seasoned professional to develop situational awareness and understanding of context? Do they help build judgment? Do they create the kinds of relationships every business is built on? These answers will help inform which tasks to automate, and which need more thought. A "yes" doesn't mean the task cannot be handed off to automation; it means the developmental value has to be preserved, somehow. The oversight role for management is to understand and enforce the right order of operations: organic brain first, neural network second. As with all complex systems, architecting experience isn't a blueprint. It's a process bound to yield different results for different organizations. Once the initial assessment is complete, ideally under the supervision of an executive with accountability, the hard work of execution, review, and adaptation begins. The good news is: there's plenty of responsibility to go around. Executive management must identify the experiences that create expertise, design a plan for succession, and own how the business will look ten years down the road. Elsewhere, HR and development teams have a responsibility to engineer the learning experiences and coaching or apprenticeship infrastructure, while managers can iterate, suggest improvements, and raise the red flag when skills aren't being developed. Tech and risk teams also have a clear role to observe AI usage, monitor costs and defect rates, and flag when automated work misses the mark. Senior professionals must keep in mind that juniors need engagement, context, and good professional models to follow, while the juniors themselves must remember to think first and ask AI second. Insurance is still early in the AI adoption process, and fortunate to have a deep bench of experienced professionals around the world, alongside ambitious newcomers. But every day, AI offers new deployment opportunities for efficiency and optimization. The greatest organizations of tomorrow will not only be able to harness those opportunities, but will also succeed in architecting experience for the next generation of world-class talent. Bob Pick November 19, 2026 Back in the '90s, I was a beast at reconciling spreadsheets. The 10 fingers I'm using to type these lines used to set my "10-key" numeric keypad ablaze. But if you're among the younger readers to come across this article, you'll have no idea what I'm talking about. And as a society, I think that's for the best. A core promise of technological advancement is to eliminate drudgery, like using a 10-key to enter vast amounts of numeric data. In property and casualty insurance, we have spent decades trying to remove mundane work from the lives of underwriters, claims professionals, and technologists. We made great strides with Robotic Process Automation (RPA), leaps with broader Intelligent Automation (IA), and now a phenomenal bound with Artificial Intelligence (AI), which promises to revolutionize the way we work. But amid the terrific change lurks an industry-scale problem. While our job definitions and related skills are morphing at an absurdly fast rate, how do we ensure that emerging talent has the opportunity to develop the depth of understanding and judgment their predecessors possess, even while AI is tending to disassociate humans from some of the traditional activities of their craft? Even where junior positions aren't disappearing, the formative skills they help develop are the easiest to automate. In insurance, applied experience and apprenticeship have built the tacit knowledge and judgment needed for success for generations. After ingesting enough submissions, you develop a second sense for when a detail looks off, or when risks that look identical stem from entirely different causes. But when this repetitive and seemingly menial work is delegated to AI, younger staff are deprived of the very task-level experiences they need to develop the business EQ, empathy, and scar tissue that will someday make them senior. What our young talent are left with are the tasks too difficult for AI, and sometimes beyond the judgment they possess. They found that heavily AI-exposed entry-level roles were seven times more likely to demand senior capabilities—like judgment, leadership, and interpersonal skills—than the jobs least exposed to AI. PwC described the trend as the "seniorization" of junior work.[2] A short-term view of AI-driven task optimization will only make the problem worse. For senior employees, more demanding tasks feel more meaningful and engaging than rote work. But the type of work that is most interesting to a seasoned professional isn't necessarily the type of work best suited to creating one. And meaningful work sounds wonderful until every task is a demanding one, and the much-needed Easy Tuesday becomes as much of a relic as my most trusty 10-digit keypad. items.title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.original_title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.rss_title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.rss_description: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 15:15 Four-year producer retention has sat near 14% for years. One overlooked cause: new producers are handed materials that promote the company but give prospects no reason to trust the person. November 19, 2026 Image Even with aptitude and personality testing, only about 14% of new financial professionals have still been under contract four years after they were hired, according to LIMRA. The losses come early. First-year retention runs from 44% to 55%, depending on who recruited the producer. When a new producer leaves within two years, the recruiting effort, the licensing, the training, and the manager's time are lost. The industry has refined selection, adjusted financing plans, and built mentoring programs. Yet the four-year number has barely moved. I spent more than 25 years in this industry as a producer, a wholesaler, and a group long-term care presenter. I've come to believe we're overlooking one piece of the problem: the gap between marketing and sales. Marketing departments produce great materials that promote the brand and its products. But those materials don't help producers distinguish themselves from colleagues who hand out the same materials. The most successful practices are built on trust. A prospect won't discuss their financial or insurance problems until they trust the producer enough to reveal highly personal information. Insurance companies have a reputation for being conservative and not on the leading edge of new technology. Perhaps it's in our DNA as managers of risk. There has always been a tension between what we can do and what we're allowed to do: a tug of war between sales and compliance. What leaders say keeps producers In a 2022 study, LIMRA and Finseca asked field and home-office leaders which factors do the most to keep new producers past year two. They named five: early activity (a fast start), a strong selection process before hiring, joint field work, quality sales skills training, and mentoring. Field leaders also listed lack of early activity among the causes of termination. Four of those five factors are about the producer: who we hire and how we train and support them. Early activity is different. It depends on two people: the producer must reach out, and the prospect has to respond. Prospects respond to people they feel a connection with. What constitutes activity? When I began, it meant 10 meetings a week with new prospects, all of them in person. You left behind a business card and a generic company brochure and hoped you'd made enough of an impression to earn a second appointment. Today, a new producer may reach out in person or virtually. Either way, the takeaway must be memorable. A business card or marketing piece that provides an experience rather than just data can raise a producer's MQ (memorability quotient) significantly. The format gap Producers are largely on their own in building trust, and the materials they're handed don't help much. The World Life Insurance Report 2027, published in September 2026 by Capgemini and LIMRA, surveyed 6,175 consumers in 18 countries. More than 40% of those considering coverage felt confused, uncertain, or unconvinced by what they found, and one in four dropped out before buying. Overly technical language was the top reason, cited by 37%. Eighty-five percent of those consumers want to interact with an advisor at some point, and two-thirds prefer a human advisor when they finalize coverage. The demand for the producer is there. The materials can get in the way instead of advancing the relationship. Research shows what helps. In an experiment by the Society of Actuaries Research Institute and RGA, summaries, FAQs, and simple icons raised comprehension by 21%. Interactive elements, such as a needs calculator, raised it by 28%. On a page that used both, adding video raised it another 15%. Imagine delivering all that through something as simple as a business card. People, both prospects and producers, differ in many ways. Finding commonality is key to establishing a relationship. Half of consumers in the Capgemini–LIMRA study said they prefer advisors with similar demographic characteristics. And in the SOA–RGA experiment, comprehension rose significantly when participants saw the presenter as credible, expert, and from a similar cultural background. As a long-term care insurance wholesaler, I often funded advisors' client events: dinners meant to turn prospects into clients. Most guests didn't know the advisor or had only a passing acquaintance with him. At one event I sponsored, the advisor spent little time presenting himself and concentrated on the features and benefits of the coverage from the company I represented. He didn't convert a single prospect, and I got zero return on my investment. The guests had no reason to trust the person in front of them, so the product never had a chance. We can't know in advance who is on the other end of a producer's outreach. Some prospects read. Some watch. Some listen. Some need to try a calculator before they believe anything. The safest approach is to offer something for each of them, with the producer's own face and voice up front. Conventional e-newsletters contribute to inbox glut Most new producers are sent out with the same tools as everyone else: a business card, perhaps a company newsletter, and a set of pre-approved PDFs. The newsletter is the piece most firms count on to keep prospects warm, and it has five weaknesses. They are too long. Attention spans are short, and screen after screen asks for more time than most readers will give. They make readers scroll to choose. Readers scroll down to see what's there, then back up to decide. Many give up first. They are mostly text. Email can carry video and interactive tools, but few firms use them. Prospects who would rather watch or listen find little to engage them. They lack creative calls to action or lead magnets of value. Readers see a "Subscribe" or "Get my 5 tips" button as permission to receive spam. They speak for the company, not the person. Prospects learn about the carrier's strength and products, but nothing about the producer who sent it. There is also a compliance cost. Approved PDFs get downloaded, forwarded, and kept long after they've been revised. A PDF attached in March can still be circulating in October, carrying last spring's disclosure. Meanwhile, new producers who need to be noticed improvise with homemade posts and flyers. Producers need to be seen, and compliance needs control. A better newsletter respects the reader's time: one page with links to no more than three pieces of content. At a glance, the reader sees each title, whether it's an article, a video, or a podcast, and about how long it will take. They choose in seconds, without scrolling, in the format they prefer. And because the pieces are links, not downloads, compliance retains more control. What a first impression could be Social media posts, newsletters, mail, and product information all have their place in the sales cycle, but on their own, none of them builds a relationship. Today's technology can ease the tension between sales and compliance. Personal profiles with video and text, built on a company-approved template, let every producer present themselves authentically by email, on social media and websites, and through "phygital" marketing: digital content delivered through physical objects such as business cards, printed materials, or promotional merchandise. An agency or firm can start with business cards, where a scan or a tap opens a short personal video scripted to feature the "who" and not the "what" along with their bio, contact information, and compliance-approved content. Data alone isn't memorable. Experiences are. The company brochure can travel the same way. Printed brochures are costly and usually end up in the circular file. The same approved piece can live behind the producer's card instead, with no reprint charges, unlimited distribution, and home-office updates that take effect everywhere at once. Stories engage far better than statistics. Say a new producer targets young couples buying their first home who need to protect their mortgage. They need life insurance, and so do growing families and pre-retirees who want to transfer wealth efficiently. A firm could offer a choice of short, approved videos, each speaking to a different audience, that drop into the same approved brochure that explains different types of life insurance. Then add a lead gate, a short form that asks for a prospect's contact details in exchange for content of value. In large organizations, lead gates usually sit on the company website, not on individual producers' pages, so the contact information goes to the company or agency. Placed in the producer's own piece, a lead gate helps a new producer build a prospect list from the first week. Put together, these elements give a new producer something memorable that builds trust: a personal profile, an approved multimedia brochure, and a way to find the people worth calling. No study yet measures the effect directly, but the evidence points the same way. What leaders can do now None of this requires a new distribution model. It requires looking at a new producer's first 90 days from the prospect's side of the table. Audit the first impression. Gather everything a new producer can send a prospect in week one. Then ask: Why would I choose this producer over another? Put the person up front. Give each new producer a short video or audio introduction about who they are, not what they do. All your producers do similar work. Who they are is what sets them apart. Cover every format. Pair each key message with something to read, something to watch or hear, and something to try. In a newsletter, that means no more than three pieces, each labeled with its format and length. Host it; don't attach it. Sharing content by link keeps the company in control and ensures only approved, up-to-date materials circulate. Watch the early signals. Lack of activity is an early warning sign, and analytics can now measure it. Managers can see which channels drive activity and which new recruits may need help sooner. Have it ready before the first appointment. A fast start depends on what the producer can share in the first week, not the first quarter. Give them something worth answering Pushing prospects with a stick instead of offering a carrot gives the industry a black eye. The better path is to make sure that when prospects look, they find a real person, in a format they can take in, with content that compliance approved and still under control. The four-year retention number has held steady for a long time. Leaders have told us that early activity matters. Our part is to give new producers something worth sharing, so a prospect's first impression is the producer and not just the company behind them. Prefer to listen? The losses come early. First-year retention runs from 44% to 55%, depending on who recruited the producer. When a new producer leaves within two years, the recruiting effort, the licensing, the training, and the manager's time are lost. The industry has refined selection, adjusted financing plans, and built mentoring programs. Yet the four-year number has barely moved. I spent more than 25 years in this industry as a producer, a wholesaler, and a group long-term care presenter. I've come to believe we're overlooking one piece of the problem: the gap between marketing and sales. Marketing departments produce great materials that promote the brand and its products. But those materials don't help producers distinguish themselves from colleagues who hand out the same materials. The most successful practices are built on trust. A prospect won't discuss their financial or insurance problems until they trust the producer enough to reveal highly personal information. Insurance companies have a reputation for being conservative and not on the leading edge of new technology. Perhaps it's in our DNA as managers of risk. There has always been a tension between what we can do and what we're allowed to do: a tug of war between sales and compliance. What leaders say keeps producers In a 2022 study, LIMRA and Finseca asked field and home-office leaders which factors do the most to keep new producers past year two. They named five: early activity (a fast start), a strong selection process before hiring, joint field work, quality sales skills training, and mentoring. Field leaders also listed lack of early activity among the causes of termination. Four of those five factors are about the producer: who we hire and how we train and support them. Early activity is different. It depends on two people: the producer must reach out, and the prospect has to respond. Prospects respond to people they feel a connection with. What constitutes activity? When I began, it meant 10 meetings a week with new prospects, all of them in person. You left behind a business card and a generic company brochure and hoped you'd made enough of an impression to earn a second appointment. Today, a new producer may reach out in person or virtually. Either way, the takeaway must be memorable. A business card or marketing piece that provides an experience rather than just data can raise a producer's MQ (memorability quotient) significantly. The format gap Producers are largely on their own in building trust, and the materials they're handed don't help much. The World Life Insurance Report 2027, published in September 2026 by Capgemini and LIMRA, surveyed 6,175 consumers in 18 countries. More than 40% of those considering coverage felt confused, uncertain, or unconvinced by what they found, and one in four dropped out before buying. Overly technical language was the top reason, cited by 37%. Eighty-five percent of those consumers want to interact with an advisor at some point, and two-thirds prefer a human advisor when they finalize coverage. The demand for the producer is there. The materials can get in the way instead of advancing the relationship. Research shows what helps. In an experiment by the Society of Actuaries Research Institute and RGA, summaries, FAQs, and simple icons raised comprehension by 21%. Interactive elements, such as a needs calculator, raised it by 28%. On a page that used both, adding video raised it another 15%. Imagine delivering all that through something as simple as a business card. People, both prospects and producers, differ in many ways. Finding commonality is key to establishing a relationship. Half of consumers in the Capgemini–LIMRA study said they prefer advisors with similar demographic characteristics. And in the SOA–RGA experiment, comprehension rose significantly when participants saw the presenter as credible, expert, and from a similar cultural background. As a long-term care insurance wholesaler, I often funded advisors' client events: dinners meant to turn prospects into clients. Most guests didn't know the advisor or had only a passing acquaintance with him. At one event I sponsored, the advisor spent little time presenting himself and concentrated on the features and benefits of the coverage from the company I represented. He didn't convert a single prospect, and I got zero return on my investment. The guests had no reason to trust the person in front of them, so the product never had a chance. We can't know in advance who is on the other end of a producer's outreach. Some prospects read. Some watch. Some listen. Some need to try a calculator before they believe anything. The safest approach is to offer something for each of them, with the producer's own face and voice up front. They are too long. Attention spans are short, and screen after screen asks for more time than most readers will give. They make readers scroll to choose. Readers scroll down to see what's there, then back up to decide. Many give up first. They are mostly text. Email can carry video and interactive tools, but few firms use them. Prospects who would rather watch or listen find little to engage them. They lack creative calls to action or lead magnets of value. Readers see a "Subscribe" or "Get my 5 tips" button as permission to receive spam. They speak for the company, not the person. Prospects learn about the carrier's strength and products, but nothing about the producer who sent it. There is also a compliance cost. Approved PDFs get downloaded, forwarded, and kept long after they've been revised. A PDF attached in March can still be circulating in October, carrying last spring's disclosure. Meanwhile, new producers who need to be noticed improvise with homemade posts and flyers. Producers need to be seen, and compliance needs control. At a glance, the reader sees each title, whether it's an article, a video, or a podcast, and about how long it will take. They choose in seconds, without scrolling, in the format they prefer. And because the pieces are links, not downloads, compliance retains more control. Today's technology can ease the tension between sales and compliance. Personal profiles with video and text, built on a company-approved template, let every producer present themselves authentically by email, on social media and websites, and through "phygital" marketing: digital content delivered through physical objects such as business cards, printed materials, or promotional merchandise. An agency or firm can start with business cards, where a scan or a tap opens a short personal video scripted to feature the "who" and not the "what" along with their bio, contact information, and compliance-approved content. Data alone isn't memorable. Experiences are. The company brochure can travel the same way. Printed brochures are costly and usually end up in the circular file. The same approved piece can live behind the producer's card instead, with no reprint charges, unlimited distribution, and home-office updates that take effect everywhere at once. Stories engage far better than statistics. Say a new producer targets young couples buying their first home who need to protect their mortgage. They need life insurance, and so do growing families and pre-retirees who want to transfer wealth efficiently. A firm could offer a choice of short, approved videos, each speaking to a different audience, that drop into the same approved brochure that explains different types of life insurance. Then add a lead gate, a short form that asks for a prospect's contact details in exchange for content of value. In large organizations, lead gates usually sit on the company website, not on individual producers' pages, so the contact information goes to the company or agency. Placed in the producer's own piece, a lead gate helps a new producer build a prospect list from the first week. Put together, these elements give a new producer something memorable that builds trust: a personal profile, an approved multimedia brochure, and a way to find the people worth calling. No study yet measures the effect directly, but the evidence points the same way. What leaders can do now None of this requires a new distribution model. Have it ready before the first appointment. A fast start depends on what the producer can share in the first week, not the first quarter. The better path is to make sure that when prospects look, they find a real person, in a format they can take in, with content that compliance approved and still under control. items.title: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps

items.rss_title: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps
items.rss_description: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps Cyber ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/18/2026 - 14:34 The $6.3 billion Binance theft bypassed private keys entirely, exposing gaps in how crypto risks are underwritten and covered. November 19, 2026 Image On Oct. 29, attackers took roughly $6.3 billion out of Binance's hot wallets in about 20 minutes. It is the largest crypto theft on record, and the FBI has tied it to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Binance has since committed to absorbing the financial impact of the incident. By Oct. 31, it reported that 98% of the affected token assets had been replenished. How it happened matters more than how much According to Binance's incident report, the campaign ran for months. One engineer installed a tampered developer tool in June. Another was compromised in September through a fake coding assignment. In October, the attackers used an internal AI tool to get into more machines and finally took control of the system that approves wallet transactions. The key detail for insurance: Binance says no private keys were stolen. The attackers didn't need them. They controlled the system that signs transactions, so it signed whatever the attackers asked. Underwriting conversations with crypto clients have long centered on keys. Where are they stored? Who holds them? How many people have to sign off? This loss shows that everything around the keys (people, laptops, software and approval systems) matters just as much. What this means for the insurance market Tougher questions. Crime and specie applications will dig into employee devices, developer tools, and internal AI tools. Underwriters will want to know who can push code into live systems and how fast a wallet can be frozen once something looks wrong. More caution on hot wallets. Offline cold storage has always been easier to insure than online hot wallets used for everyday withdrawals. After watching billions leave hot wallets in minutes, insurers will be more careful about how much limit they put there and what they charge. More disputes over which policy pays. Crypto losses tend to fall between cyber and crime policies, and this attack sits right on the line. Cyber or crime? Four common mix-ups "We have cyber, so a hack is covered." Cyber pays for the cleanup - forensics, legal advice, customer notices, data lawsuits, and lost income while systems are down. Most cyber policies exclude the theft or transfer of funds, and many exclude digital assets. Cyber may pay for the investigation but not the stolen assets. "We have crime, so theft is covered." A standard crime policy protects money, securities and other property. Without an endorsement, crypto may not clearly fit. Specie policies often cover cold storage only, with hot wallets excluded or sublimited. "Computer fraud and funds transfer fraud are the same thing." They aren't. Computer fraud usually needs a hacker to change data or force a transfer. Funds transfer fraud usually involves fake instructions sent to a bank. An exchange signing its own blockchain transaction may not fit neatly into either. "Our people were tricked, so social engineering coverage applies." Expect a debate. Social engineering coverage usually responds when an employee is fooled into sending money, often with a small sublimit. Here, engineers were tricked into installing bad software, not sending funds. What brokers should review before the next renewal Map the gaps. Lay the crime, specie, cyber, tech E&O, and D&O policies side by side and walk through this scenario. Who pays for the stolen assets, the forensics, and the lawsuits? Check the "other insurance" clauses, since cyber and crime policies sometimes each point to the other. Compare limits to real exposure. Ask how much the client keeps in hot wallets on a normal day and a busy day, then compare that to the limit they're buying. Talk about the reserve fund. Many exchanges keep their own fund to repay customers. That isn't insurance, and if it's held in crypto, its value can drop right when it's needed. Don't forget D&O. Lawsuits and regulators usually follow a large loss, often in more than one country. Directors and officers will want to know their coverage holds up. Looking ahead There is some good news here. About $2.85 billion of the stolen funds has been frozen or intercepted, mostly stablecoins whose issuers can block them, and Binance has said customers will be covered. Insurance capacity for digital asset companies keeps growing. More insurers are willing to write crime, specie and D&O for crypto businesses than a few years ago, and one event shouldn't reverse that. But more capacity doesn't mean easier terms. This single loss accounts for nearly three-quarters of the crypto hacking losses recorded this year. Headline events like this make underwriters more careful. Expect longer applications, more underwriting meetings and a closer look at how controls work day to day. Vague answers will cost you. For brokers, the job is easy to describe and hard to do. Understand how the client actually operates, not just where the keys are kept, and make sure the coverage matches. The clients who can show their work will get the best of the new capacity. The next renewal is the right time to start that conversation. Ben Slagis

This loss shows that everything around the keys (people, laptops, software and approval systems) matters just as much. What this means for the insurance market Tougher questions. Crime and specie applications will dig into employee devices, developer tools, and internal AI tools. Underwriters will want to know who can push code into live systems and how fast a wallet can be frozen once something looks wrong. More caution on hot wallets. Offline cold storage has always been easier to insure than online hot wallets used for everyday withdrawals. After watching billions leave hot wallets in minutes, insurers will be more careful about how much limit they put there and what they charge. More disputes over which policy pays. Crypto losses tend to fall between cyber and crime policies, and this attack sits right on the line. Cyber or crime? Four common mix-ups "We have cyber, so a hack is covered." Cyber pays for the cleanup - forensics, legal advice, customer notices, data lawsuits, and lost income while systems are down. Most cyber policies exclude the theft or transfer of funds, and many exclude digital assets. Cyber may pay for the investigation but not the stolen assets. "We have crime, so theft is covered." A standard crime policy protects money, securities and other property. Without an endorsement, crypto may not clearly fit. Specie policies often cover cold storage only, with hot wallets excluded or sublimited. "Computer fraud and funds transfer fraud are the same thing." They aren't. Computer fraud usually needs a hacker to change data or force a transfer. Funds transfer fraud usually involves fake instructions sent to a bank. An exchange signing its own blockchain transaction may not fit neatly into either. "Our people were tricked, so social engineering coverage applies." Expect a debate. Social engineering coverage usually responds when an employee is fooled into sending money, often with a small sublimit. Here, engineers were tricked into installing bad software, not sending funds. What brokers should review before the next renewal Map the gaps. Lay the crime, specie, cyber, tech E&O, and D&O policies side by side and walk through this scenario. Who pays for the stolen assets, the forensics, and the lawsuits? Check the "other insurance" clauses, since cyber and crime policies sometimes each point to the other. Compare limits to real exposure. Ask how much the client keeps in hot wallets on a normal day and a busy day, then compare that to the limit they're buying. Talk about the reserve fund. Many exchanges keep their own fund to repay customers. That isn't insurance, and if it's held in crypto, its value can drop right when it's needed. Don't forget D&O. Lawsuits and regulators usually follow a large loss, often in more than one country. Directors and officers will want to know their coverage holds up. Looking ahead There is some good news here. About $2.85 billion of the stolen funds has been frozen or intercepted, mostly stablecoins whose issuers can block them, and Binance has said customers will be covered. Insurance capacity for digital asset companies keeps growing. More insurers are willing to write crime, specie and D&O for crypto businesses than a few years ago, and one event shouldn't reverse that. But more capacity doesn't mean easier terms. This single loss accounts for nearly three-quarters of the crypto hacking losses recorded this year. Headline events like this make underwriters more careful. Expect longer applications, more underwriting meetings and a closer look at how controls work day to day. Vague answers will cost you. For brokers, the job is easy to describe and hard to do. Understand how the client actually operates, not just where the keys are kept, and make sure the coverage matches. The clients who can show their work will get the best of the new capacity. The next renewal is the right time to start that conversation. Get Involved Our authors are what set Insurance Thought Leadership apart. Learn More Ben Slagis Ben Slagis Ben Slagis is the digital risk practice leader at IMA Financial Group , a North American insurance brokerage firm specializing in risk management, employee benefits and investment advisory services. items.title: When Customers Get Their Own Chatbot Agent
items.original_title: When Customers Get Their Own Chatbot Agent
items.rss_title: When Customers Get Their Own Chatbot Agent
items.rss_description: When Customers Get Their Own Chatbot Agent PaulCarroll Sun, 11/22/2026 - 21:48 For some years now, I've been developing what I call the Laws of Zero. The notion is that the price of certain digital goods looks like it's headed toward zero if you map the cost curve out five or 10 years -- computing power, communication, sensors and cameras, in particular, have all seen exponential declines. So you should plan as though you will have an infinite supply of those goods. Thinking about zero cost has been a useful exercise for businesses... but AI is now driving the cost of intelligence toward zero, too, which will provide what feel like infinite amounts of it to customers. They're going to use it. We've already seen how AI has changed online search and started to alter many shopping behaviors. But AI agents will also mean that there will be essentially zero marginal cost for customers who want to request an update on an insurance claim, who want to complain, who want to challenge a bill, or who want any other sort of service. Meta's recent announcement of its Muse personal agent is just the start. The floodgates are about to open. Let's have a look. The positive response to Meta's announcement shows that the clock has started ticking on the trend toward vastly more customer service contacts. There will be the usual sorts of growing pains as the technology is being adopted -- there have already been reports of the AI agent getting into user data, such as bank records, that were supposed to be off limits -- so you won't be inundated right away. But the change is coming, so you might as well start planning. Think about all the calls you don't make and emails you don't send about a product or service you've bought because you don't have the time or just don't want to deal with the hassle. Lots of companies make considerable profit off the fact that people don't get around to canceling subscriptions. Then imagine what happens when someone can just tell an agent to make that contact -- or when the agent simply does the work on its own because it knows you want it to. That ease of contact issue hit home for me a couple of months ago, when my older daughter wrote an article for the Travel section of the Wall Street Journal. In my 17 years at the WSJ, the most letters I got on an article was maybe 300, and my daughter beat that on her first try. There were close to 300 comments on the article, and she received maybe 200 emails routed through the WSJ. The reason -- other than the fact that she wrote a great piece -- was that readers back in the 1990s had to type out a letter, surely in a formal style, use White-Out to fix any errors, find the right address in the paper's masthead, address the envelope, put a stamp on it and mail it. With my daughter, an online reader just had to hit the "comment" button or the "email" button and start typing. Ease of access will cause the same sort of increase in contacts for insurance companies. Meta even used a question about an insurance bill as an example of what Muse Wonder can do in an initial promotional video. (The example begins at the 2:27 mark here .) A couple of initial thoughts on how to get ready: For starters, you want to do everything you can to reduce the need for customers to wonder about anything. Amazon, in its early days, treated every contact by a customer as signifying a failure, and you should adopt that same mindset. I realize that will be far harder in insurance, with its complex processes and contracts, than it is in book selling. Still, every question that doesn't arise is one you don't have to figure out how to answer. Every update you provide is one the customer or their AI agent doesn't have to request. You'll also want to think about how to make your systems as accessible as possible to AI -- within privacy restrictions, regulation, etc. That effort will include sorting out which queries are from an AI, so you can have your AI deal with the customers' agents as much as possible and only bring in your human staff when necessary. The sooner you get started planning for the onslaught of customer inquiries, the better prepared you'll be. Zero is a magic number. Free is an unbeatable cost. Cheers, Paul P.S. If you're intrigued by my favorite topic, the Laws of Zero, the most complete explanation I've developed is in a book I wrote with Chunka Mui and Tim Andrews, " A Brief History of a Perfect Future: Inventing the World We Can Proudly Leave Our Kids by 2050 ." Image Paul Carroll While the focus to this point has been on customers potentially using AI agents to shop for insurance, people will also use them to demand much more service. Much more. items.extracted_text: Arch finalises $162m Bellemeade Re 2026-1 mortgage ILS, plus $40.5m direct reinsurance - Artemis.bm Arch finalises $162m Bellemeade Re 2026-1 mortgage ILS, plus $40.5m direct reinsurance 25th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Arch Capital Group has now secured the targeted $162 million of capital markets backed reinsurance from its new Bellemeade Re 2026-1 Ltd. issuance of mortgage insurance-linked notes, while also securing a further $40.5 million of direct reinsurance alongside the deal. The transaction, which we first reported on earlier this month here , now becomes the 23rd Bellemeade Re mortgage insurance-linked securities issuance and the 21st since Arch Capital became the sponsor, on behalf of its two ceding mortgage insurers Arch Mortgage Insurance Company and United Guaranty Residential Insurance Company. This Bellemeade Re 2026-1 issuance of mortgage insurance-linked securities is the first from Arch Capital in one year and only the second mortgage ILS transaction to come to market of 2026 so far. Roughly one year ago, Arch Capital successfully secured $199.3 million of reinsurance through the Bellemeade Re 2025-1 Ltd. issuance . Arch Capital, as the longest-standing sponsor of these mortgage ILS deals, continues to utilise them as a way to source efficient and diversifying reinsurance capacity from capital market investors. Read about every mortgage ILS issuance by filtering our Deal Directory . After the Bellemeade Re 2026-1 mortgage insurance-linked notes issuance closed yesterday, Arch Mortgage Insurance Company announced today that it actually secured $202.5 million of indemnity reinsurance on a pool representing approximately $55 billion of mortgages via the special purpose reinsurer. $162 million in bonds were issued, while an additional $40.503 million in direct mortgage reinsurance was also placed with a panel of reinsurers via the Bellemeade transaction. The reinsurance largely covers a portfolio of mortgage insurance policies issued by Arch MI and affiliates primarily from September 2025 through October 2026. Across the now 23 transactions under the Bellemeade program, Arch has now secured nearly $10 billion in indemnity reinsurance protection for its mortgage insurance underwriting business from the capital markets and reinsurers. “We have issued at least one Bellemeade transaction a year since 2015, and we remain committed to the program as an important part of Arch’s risk and capital management strategy,” explained Jennifer Weiss, VP of Structured Capital and Reinsurance for Arch MI. “We are very pleased with the execution of this transaction. Strong investor engagement allowed us to achieve attractive execution across the capital structure, while maintaining an amortization structure aligned with our PMIERs capital requirements.” You can read all about the Bellemeade Re 2026-1 Ltd. mortgage insurance-linked securities transaction and every other mortgage ILS deal by filtering our extensive Artemis Deal Directory . items.title: What Do AI Damage Estimates Bring to the Claims Table?
items.original_title: What Do AI Damage Estimates Bring to the Claims Table?
items.rss_title: What Do AI Damage Estimates Bring to the Claims Table?
items.rss_description: Bringing two sides on anything together seems less than likely in an increasingly polarized world. But some believe that artificial intelligence has a chance to bring two opposites closer to an unlikely agreement. AI-generated damage estimates could, through cold, hard …
items.extracted_text: What Do AI Damage Estimates Bring to the Claims Table? Article 0 Comments Bringing two sides on anything together seems less than likely in an increasingly polarized world. But some believe that artificial intelligence has a chance to bring two opposites closer to an unlikely agreement. AI-generated damage estimates could, through cold, hard data, bring policyholders and payers closer together on insurance claims payouts. Joe Ledbetter, a senior developer at Encircle, a claims app, believes the first steps toward a closer agreement between the two parties are already being taken. “There is AI usage on both ends, on both sides of the aisle, and they’re coming to a convergence within the claims process that is demonstrating a more accurate dollar value between the two parties,” Ledbetter said. “So, AI, on both sides, unintentionally, when they come together, they are actually more aligned than they were with just two humans assembling files trying to get aligned.” Related: APCIA Says Claims Data Standards in Works to Better Combat Criticism Ledbetter said his firm is putting out roughly 1,000 AI scopes a day by taking field data and running it through their AI, which produces the entire scope of work and then puts that into Xactimate. “So, what I can tell you is that the contractor’s data is 90% more accurate today and more complete today than it was without any of these tools,” Ledbetter said. “And so, the contractor side is seeing far more accurate estimates and scopes being produced on job files because AI is in the background making sure they don’t miss anything.” Simplifying the claims process with AI and technology has become a ubiquitous industry news refrain, but that doesn’t mean everyone is going to be happy with these developments. According to Mark Garrett, a director in the insurance intelligence and analytics practice at J.D. Power, technology may improve estimates and streamline processes, but claimants do not always have a better experience. J.D. Power surveys have found that, in some cases, customers feel that the photos they take and submit through a claims app go unused or unseen. “So, what I can tell you is from the customer process standpoint, it’s a big problem if they go through all the hassle submitting photos,” Garrett said. He said claimants are more likely to feel they went through unnecessary effort to get compensated for a loss when they are asked to take additional steps after submitting photos and claim details, such as taking their vehicle to a shop for a final estimate. Related: As AI Laws Proliferate, Liability and Coverage Questions Multiply “What that can do, though, is create huge slowdowns in the process,” Garrett said. “If they tear down the car, the shop’s starting to work on things and they realize ‘Oh yeah all this was missed in that AI estimate,’ that alone can add days. We’re not talking about an hour or same-day approval. We’re talking about five or six days for a carrier to get back to the shop, then maybe they ask questions and the shop’s got to respond back.” Nuha Hashem, co-founder and chief technology officer of Cozmo AI, believes that all the steps involved in the traditional claims process are one reason the two parties’ estimates often come in so far apart. She describes that process as someone reporting damage to an adjuster by phone or digitally, followed by a manual sketch of the damage and then a digital version of that sketch. Photos must be uploaded with notes, which are handed to a desk estimator for review. That all goes into Xactimate, where line items and codes are entered. “The work that these people are doing right now, they don’t have to go through all of this manual work,” Hashem said. “They just have to focus on talking with the customer, making sure the work is done to the standards.” Timothy Wieneke, president and managing director of Wieneke Group, which provides property claims services, decided to try an experiment that led to him creating an AI-based tool that generated estimates in about 30 seconds. “Its accuracy was about 90-95% on roofs,” he wrote in response to a reporter’s LinkedIn post asking for insight and comments from claims professionals about their experience with AI damage estimates. That wasn’t his only experiment with AI and damage estimates, a tale he shared as a point of caution. “The bigger thing was what I learned in the process of making it. I can tell you, in depth, how to manipulate AI to create estimates to look like whatever you want,” said Wieneke, who conducted the AI experiment as part of a conference presentation on AI. “I showed specific prompts that instruct AI to manipulate estimate results. I can make AI manipulate the same scope of work down by 50% or triple it with the right prompting.” The lesson he came away with is that the industry needs to “get out ahead of AI.” “I’m starting to see it being used to create estimates that look legitimate but raise serious questions,” he added. Ledbetter said AI damage estimates are not only bringing valuations closer but also helping to improve documentation. He’s already seeing contractors improving on this. “They’re putting really good claim package together with estimates and PDF reports and drying logs and photos,” he said. On the other side, he is seeing carriers working to create efficiencies, building streamlined intake processes. “Then they have an LLM, an AI tool, read all of that context and digest it and then what those tools are traditionally looking for are the gaps or the holes or the missing information,” he said. Ledbetter said a carrier may flag an estimate that bills for three days of drying when the claim file contains documentation for only the first two days. The missing documentation for the third day does not necessarily mean the work was not performed, but it creates a gap for the carrier to review. Alok Kumar, co-founder of Cozmo AI, believes it’s not just the data that will better align claimants and insurers. He believes the push and pull between the two will balance out with a structured data set aligned with industry standards, laws, regulations and contracts. “So, I believe once you have common datasets, then it’s a black and white,” Kumar said. “Today, it’s not a black and white. That’s because a 10-year-experience human estimator has a different point of view than a one-year-experience human estimator. So, when you can actually bridge that gap with pure data and numbers, then it ceases to be gray or spectrums of gray.” Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.extracted_text: Alignment and transparency key to sustainable casualty sidecar capacity: Artex CEO Faries - Artemis.bm Alignment and transparency key to sustainable casualty sidecar capacity: Artex CEO Faries 26th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard As momentum continues to build within the casualty sidecar market, Kathleen Faries of Artex Capital Solutions has outlined that pairing strong underwriting fundamentals with greater structural transparency and sponsor-investor alignment could create a sustainable force of casualty capacity and a more durable relationship between the insurance and asset-management markets. Faries made these comments in Artex Capital Solutions’ latest Alternative View report. In the report, the insurance-linked securities market service provider and insurance management specialist, highlighted how reinsurance sidecars and private ILS transactions have experienced considerable growth throughout 2026. Earlier this year, rating agency S&P Global highlighted a structural shift in the sidecar market, with casualty reinsurance sidecars growing to account for approximately 10% of total sidecar capacity. In fact, throughout the past couple of years, sidecars have increased in both the size and number of transactions, with an increasing share of that growth coming from the casualty market. At the beginning of 2026, QBE Re, the international reinsurance arm of the global insurance group, sponsored its first casualty reinsurance sidecar vehicle, securing over $550 million in fully collateralised quota share reinsurance through George Street Re. Everest Group also launched its first casualty re/insurance sidecar earlier this year too in Annapurna Re, deploying $600 million of third-party capital through the structure, while Stone Point Insurance Solutions served as the anchor investor backing the venture. As a reminder, you can find details of numerous reinsurance sidecar investments and transactions in our directory of collateralized reinsurance sidecars transactions . Artex’s report emphasises that an investor-focused approach to sidecar design responding to investors’ interest in vehicles that prioritise frequency and duration of losses rather than loss severity, has helped make this growth in the sidecar market possible. “Sponsors have enhanced structures to provide greater transparency into reserve development and clearer pathways for capital release. These features address a key investor requirement: confidence that capital can be returned within a defined timeframe, typically seven to ten years, despite the long-tail nature of the underlying exposures,” Artex’s report explains. The ILS market service provider further emphasised that structures able to scale will ultimately be those in which sponsors and investors share a clear understanding and alignment on several key areas. These include when and how capital will be returned and how the tail will be managed how assets are managed and invested how performance is measured and how risk behaviours and reserves are calculated. “Casualty’s long duration creates an investable asset pool alongside underwriting risk – a total-return opportunity that attracts asset managers, particularly those with private-credit expertise in longer-duration assets, cash flows and asset-liability management. That said, the insurance fundamentals should still come first disciplined underwriting, strong actuarial and claims capabilities, and a very clear understanding of how the liabilities can develop,” commented Kathleen Faries, Chief Executive Officer, Artex Capital Solutions She added: “Get that combination right, and casualty sidecars can move beyond episodic reinsurance capital – providing sponsors with committed, nontraditional capacity and investors with underwriting and investment returns. items.extracted_text: PERILS finalises industry loss estimate for Queensland & New South Wales SCS at AU $3.1bn - Artemis.bm PERILS finalises industry loss estimate for Queensland & New South Wales SCS at AU $3.1bn 26th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Catastrophe data aggregator PERILS has published its fourth and final industry loss estimate for the severe convective storms that impacted Queensland and New South Wales between November 21st to 27th, 2025, placing the insurance market loss at AU $3.132 billion, a 6% increase from the firm’s third loss estimate. We covered PERILS’ initial industry loss estimate for these severe convective storms back in January, where losses at the time had reached AU $2.663 billion. In late February, PERILS released its second loss estimate, three months after the event end date, lifting the total almost 11% to AU $2.95 billion. PERILS then released its third loss estimate in late May, six months after the event end date, where the loss total had slightly decreased to AU $2.943 billion. Now, the final industry loss estimate for the event has increased by roughly 6% from the third loss estimate to AU $3.132 billion, PERILS has reported today. PERILS also explained that its loss estimate is based on data gathered from impacted insurers from the majority of the Australian insurance market and includes losses from property and motor lines of business. PERILS’ data shows that property losses contributed a staggering 89% of the total industry loss, while the remaining 11% came from motor losses. The event primarily affected the states of Queensland, which contributed 93% of the total industry loss, while New South Wales accounted 7% of the loss total. “Severe convective storm activity affected large areas of Australia’s east coast over the period from 21 to 27 November 2025. The event brought extensive hail, damaging winds, and heavy rainfall extending from South East Queensland through to New South Wales,” PERILS explained. According to the catastrophe data aggregator, the most significant losses were associated with storms on November 24th, where exceptionally large hailstones reached up to 14cm in diameter, and struck parts of South East Queensland during the afternoon and evening. Darryl Pidcock, Head of Asia Pacific & Cyber at PERILS, commented: “This was the second and more significant severe convective storm event within a month, with industry losses across both events totalling AUD 4,752 million.” Pidcock continued: “It demonstrates the loss potential of hail-driven events affecting major population centres, especially in South East Queensland, a region that experiences frequent storms during the spring storm season. Whilst there were large hail stones in some areas, heavy winds and torrential rainfall also caused considerable damage especially to residential properties which was the primary component of the overall losses. “This differs from other hailstorms where motor losses can often constitute the largest part of the losses. items.extracted_text: Investors maintaining ILS allocations shows where they see relative value: Sapelza, Lumen Re - Artemis.bm Investors maintaining ILS allocations shows where they see relative value: Sapelza, Lumen Re 26th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard As institutional investors constantly compare catastrophe risk with private credit, infrastructure, emerging market debt, as well as other alternatives, the fact that many continue to consistently maintain their insurance-linked securities (ILS) allocations heavily shows where they see value today, Klaus Sapelza, Chief Underwriting Officer at Lumen Re told Artemis. Lumen Re is the main Bermuda-domiciled rated reinsurance underwriting vehicle of specialist insurance-linked securities manager LGT ILS Partners. Sapelza spoke to Artemis around the key conference season and discussed a number of key topics, such as the crucial role ILS managers play towards helping investors make allocation decisions during market cycles, as well as how he views the ILS market’s continued expansion into casualty and cyber lines. A common view across the market is that ILS capital drives the reinsurance cycle by flooding in after good years and undermining pricing discipline. However, Sapelza sees it differently. “Capital allocation decisions are not made by ILS managers. They are made by pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, endowments, family offices and other institutions. These investors compare ILS with other alternative asset classes. If expected ILS returns become less attractive than those of other alternatives, capital will move elsewhere, although not necessarily overnight,” the CUO explained. The CUO continued: “The concept that institutional investors are unaware of where the reinsurance market sits in the cycle has never felt particularly convincing to us. Most of the investors we speak with focus on relative value. In some respects, we would even argue that ILS capital can be quite disciplined. It is not tied to market share, client relationships or strategic ambitions. When returns no longer justify the assumed risk, capital can leave.” “The reinsurance cycle matters. But so does the broader investment cycle. Investors are constantly comparing catastrophe risk with private credit, infrastructure, emerging market debt and other alternatives. The fact that many continue to maintain their ILS allocations indicates where they see value today.” Moreover, the overall market consensus is that reinsurance pricing will further soften by 2027, which according to Sapelza, should not concern ILS investors. “Investors are less concerned with whether pricing will be lower in 2027 compared to 2026 than with whether returns remain competitive with other allocation opportunities. Currently, we are not hearing that the alternatives are obviously more attractive. Private credit spreads have tightened. High-yield markets are relatively expensive by historical standards. Emerging market debt comes with a different set of risks. “Against this backdrop, catastrophe reinsurance still offers short duration and relatively low correlation with broader financial markets. One factor that receives less attention is retained earnings. Even without fresh inflows, successful underwriting years generate additional deployable capital because earnings are typically reinvested. It is one reason why softening cycles can develop faster than people expect,” Sapelza told Artemis. We then asked the CUO to explain that if investors make allocation decisions, what role does an ILS manager effectively play towards helping them navigate the market cycle? Sapelza noted that investors expect ILS managers to source business, underwrite risk and provide them with market insights, which would include identifying less attractive opportunities, but stressed that much like any asset management business, there must be a balance between growing assets and maintaining discipline. “We firmly believe that manager credibility matters more than asset growth. When conditions soften, managers can either assume more risk to defend returns or remain selective and accept that returns may moderate. Investors want appropriate compensation for risk. They should take a close look at a manager when gathering and retaining assets becomes a higher priority than protecting returns,” Sapelza said. Reinsurance sidecars and retrocession quota shares have gained heavy momentum across the market throughout the last year. However, we asked Sapelza to explain whether he believes this portrays a healthy development for the market whilst it’s in the midst of a softening cycle? “Sidecars have an important place in the market. Historically, they have allowed reinsurers to bring in additional capital when capacity was scarce, while retaining meaningful net exposure alongside investors whose interests are aligned,” the CUO said. “Today, investors need to understand whether the sponsoring reinsurer is increasing third-party capital while maintaining its own commitment, or whether the reinsurer is reducing net exposure by transferring risk the company no longer wants in a softer market, while collecting a fee to subsidize the remaining net book. Those are very different situations. More broadly, sidecars increase available capacity. “When the market is already well capitalized, this additional supply of course contributes to pricing pressure. That does not mean sidecars are inherently problematic. The question is whether the incentives and economics remain aligned between investors and the sponsoring reinsurer.” Throughout the last few years, the insurance-linked securities market has expanded into casualty, cyber, and other long-tail lines to deploy the growing asset pool. Cyber has been a key expansion area, with the ILS market seeing its first 144A cyber catastrophe bond transaction in late 2023, and since then the market has seen a total of 14 cyber-related cat bonds. Additionally, the casualty ILS space has gained considerable momentum in recent years, as institutional investors continue to display heightened interest in longer-duration yield opportunities, which has helped drive a surge in casualty-oriented structures. Whilst this shift in direction is bringing more momentum to the broader ILS space, Sapelza argues that these strategies are moving the asset class away from what originally attracted capital. “The original attraction of ILS was fairly simple. Investors supported the insurance industry in managing extreme scenarios and gained access to short-tail catastrophe risk with a relatively clear loss trigger, limited duration, attractive returns and diversification benefits. However, casualty, cyber and other long-tail risks are very different from that initial proposition,” Sapelza said. He continued: “Specifically regarding casualty, a block of long-tail business is often passed to asset managers who aggressively work the collateral pool to compensate for potential reserve deterioration. This may be a legitimate investment strategy, but it is simply structured finance, not ILS. Some of these novel strategies may prove successful, and some investors may genuinely want this diversification. “However, these strategies move the asset class away from what originally attracted capital. Investors should ask themselves whether these strategies are developed because they solve a real problem and offer true value to investors, or if they are developed simply because managers need to allocate a growing pool of capital. Those two things do not always coincide.” To end, Sapelza shared that Lumen Re remains focused on maintaining broadly consistent risk levels over time and accepting that returns may moderate during the cycle. “When pricing softens, there is a temptation to move down the risk curve or take on more exposure to defend returns. We focus on maintaining broadly consistent risk levels over time and accept that returns may moderate during the cycle. “We spend a lot of time helping investors assess ILS against the other opportunities in the alternatives market. The allocation decision is theirs, but it should be made with a clear understanding of relative value. Having exclusive access to a rated carrier gives LGT ILS Partners flexibility. It allows LGT ILS Partners to access parts of the market that are difficult to reach through a fully collateralized structure and to be selective about where the firm deploys capital. The focus is on underwriting quality and allocating capital where the risk-reward balance still makes sense,” Sapelza concludes.
